o: Aggregate per creator: total views and the best video (highest views, tie broken by lexicographically smallest id). Then output entries for creators achieving the global maximum total. Example 1: alice totals 10 with best id "one" (5 views, "one" < "three"), bob totals 10 with "two" → both appear. Example 2: alice's best is "b" (tie 2 views, "b" < "c"). With n ≤ 10⁵ and short strings, a single hash-map pass is ideal.
k: One dictionary maps creator → [totalViews, bestViews, bestId].
Update best video with (views, id) comparison: higher views wins, ties go to smaller id.
Track the global max total in the same pass, then filter.

a.i: Maintain per-creator aggregates while scanning the videos once; afterwards collect creators whose total equals the maximum.
s: For each video: add views to the creator's total; replace their best video if (views > bestViews) or (views == bestViews and id < bestId).
Collect [creator, bestId] for every creator with total == maxTotal.
a.t: O(n·L) — one pass with string comparisons of length ≤ 5.

a.i: Sort video indices by (creator, −views, id), then sweep to compute totals and pick each creator's first video; finally sort creators by total to find the max group.
s: Create index array sorted by creator asc, views desc, id asc.
Sweep to accumulate totals and record each creator's first (best) video.
Find max total and emit matching creators.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort.

w: Prefer Approach 1 (single pass, no comparator bugs). Pitfalls: duplicate ids across videos (compare full records, treat videos as distinct), tie-breaking direction on ids (lexicographically smallest), and 64-bit totals in Java/C++. Follow-up: top-k creators, or sliding-window popularity over time.
